content: The hydrophobic effect refers to the tendency of non-polar molecules to aggregate in an aqueous environment and to engage in similar intramolecular interactions. The term originates from the Greek words hydro (water) and phobos (fear), describing the apparent repulsion between water and hydrocarbons. On a macroscopic scale, the hydrophobic effect is evident when oil and water are mixed, forming separate layers, or when water beads on hydrophobic surfaces like waxy leaves. At the molecular level, this effect plays a critical role in biological systems, driving processes such as protein folding, protein-protein interactions, the formation of lipid bilayer membranes, nucleic acid structures, and protein-small molecule interactions. According to the solvophobic theory in Reversed Phase Chromatography (RPC), the hydrophobic effect is driven by the loss of hydrogen bonding and the high entropic cost of forming a cavity around non-polar molecules. These losses are minimized by forcing non-polar molecules to aggregate. Amphiphiles are molecules that contain both hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions. Detergents, which are composed of amphiphiles, enable the solubilization of hydrophobic molecules in water by forming micelles and bilayers, as seen in soap bubbles. Amphiphiles are also essential components of cell membranes, where amphiphilic phospholipids prevent the mixing of the cell's internal aqueous environment with external water. In protein folding, the hydrophobic effect is crucial for understanding the structure of proteins containing hydrophobic amino acids such as alanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, phenylalanine, and methionine. Most folded proteins have a hydrophobic core, where side chain packing stabilizes the folded state, while charged or polar side chains are exposed to the solvent, interacting with surrounding water molecules. The primary driving force behind protein folding is the minimization of hydrophobic side chains exposed to water, although recent theories have re-evaluated the role of hydrogen bonding in this process. The energetics of DNA tertiary structure assembly are also primarily driven by the hydrophobic effect, rather than Watson-Crick base pairing, which governs sequence selectivity. However, stacking interactions between aromatic bases also contribute significantly to DNA structure. The thermodynamics of the hydrophobic effect can be quantified using the transfer free energy ((Delta G_{text{t}})) of a non-polar molecule from a non-polar solvent to an aqueous solvent. At room temperature, (Delta G_{text{t}}) is positive, with the enthalpy component ((Delta H_{text{t}})) being approximately zero and the entropy component ((-TDelta S_{text{t}})) being negative. This indicates that the hydrophobic effect is entropy-driven at room temperature. The heat capacity change in transfer ((Delta C_{p,text{t}})) is positive for hydrophobic molecules, contrasting with the negative value observed for hydrophilic molecules. A hydrophobic substance in water disrupts the structure of pure water molecules, which naturally adopt a configuration that maximizes entropy. The hydrophobic molecule creates a cavity as it cannot interact electrostatically with water molecules, reducing entropy. When multiple cavities are present, the surface area of disruption increases, leaving fewer free water molecules. To counteract this, water molecules push the hydrophobic molecules together, forming a cage structure around them. This cage has a smaller surface area than the total surface area of the individual cavities, thereby maximizing the number of free water molecules and increasing entropy. Thus, the hydrophobic effect can also be understood as the lipophobicity of water.
